definition: Counterproductive means having the opposite of the intended, useful effect; backfiring instead of helping.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word counterproductive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know counterproductive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Padlocking the suggestion box proved counterproductive: complaints doubled once employees felt silenced.
An unproductive effort simply fails to accomplish anything, while a counterproductive one actively pushes the goal further away.
Counterproductive actions set back the goal they were meant to serve, but ruinous actions destroy the whole enterprise beyond repair.

Self-defeating describes a plan or habit that carries its own failure inside it — the very design works against the goal. Counterproductive is the verdict on results: the action, whatever its design, ended up pushing the goal further away. A strategy can look perfectly sound and still prove counterproductive; self-defeating says the flaw was built in.

Self-sabotaging means actively undermining your own effort, and it hints at inner conflict — a person wrecking their own chances. Counterproductive carries no such psychology: it simply reports that an action backfired, achieving the opposite of what it was meant to do. A nervous speaker's constant excuses are self-sabotaging; a badly timed rule is merely counterproductive.

After a losing streak, a basketball coach began punishing every defeat with extra two-hour drills late into the night.
The players grew so exhausted that their shooting got worse, their tempers got shorter, and the team dropped even more games.
A plan meant to build winners was actually manufacturing losses.
The assistant coach finally said aloud what everyone suspected: the punishment drills were counterproductive.
The extra drills were meant to improve the team but produced the opposite effect, more losses, which is exactly what counterproductive describes.

Frustrated by rush-hour backups, the town council widened Route 9 from two lanes to four, promising commuters relief within a year.
For a month the new lanes flowed; then drivers who had been taking the train noticed, and switched.
By spring the widened road carried nearly twice the cars at the same crawl, and the train line, starved of riders, cut its schedule.
Traffic engineers called the project counterproductive rather than merely wasteful: the town had spent millions and ended up further from free-flowing streets than before the first shovel.
The council's own report conceded the point in one line -- the cure had fed the disease.
